notes.meaning: God tells Ezekiel to use a sharp sword like a barber's razor and shave off all his hair and beard. The sword stands for the enemy army of Babylon. Shaving meant disgrace and deep mourning. For a priest like Ezekiel it also meant losing the sign that he was set apart for God. The scales show that God's judgment is exact and fair, down to the last hair.

The hair is split three ways, and each part stands for the people of Jerusalem. One third is burned inside the model city Ezekiel had drawn in chapter 4. That stands for those who would die of hunger and sickness during the siege. Another third is struck with the sword, for those killed in the fighting. The last third is scattered to the wind, for those taken captive or who fled to Egypt and other lands. God's sword following them means that running away would not save them.

Ezekiel ties a few strands into the folds of his robe, the way people tucked away something they did not want to lose. This pictures a small remnant, a few survivors God would keep. Many writers link them to the small group left in the land under the governor Gedaliah after the city fell. God kept a few so that His promises to His people would still stand. Even these few would still face hard trials.

Even some of those saved hairs are thrown into the fire. Those who seemed to escape were still not safe. After Gedaliah was murdered, the people left behind were scattered. Some fled to Egypt and suffered there. The final fall of Jerusalem also crushed the hopes of the exiles far away, like a fire spreading to all Israel.

Now God explains the sign plainly: "This is Jerusalem." He had placed her in the middle of the great nations of the world, where everyone could see her. She was meant to be like a lamp on a stand, spreading God's light to the nations around her. Great privilege brings great responsibility.

Instead of keeping God's laws, Jerusalem rebelled against them, more than the nations did. Her sin was worse because she had God's word and knew His will, while the nations were still in the dark. The people did not just break God's laws. They twisted them into a cover for wickedness. When the best thing goes bad, it becomes the worst.

God says His people have been more unruly than the nations around them. They did not even live up to the nations' standard. The nations stayed loyal to their false gods, but Israel walked away from the true God. Some add that Israel also fell below the nations in plain, everyday goodness.

"I Myself am against you" is a fearful word. God, who had defended Jerusalem, now stands against her. Babylon's army would be only the tool in His hand. He would judge her openly, in front of all the nations. They thought He was asleep, but He would show He is the Judge.

Because of their disgusting idol worship, God would punish Jerusalem in a way He had never done before. Lamentations calls it worse than what happened to Sodom. Many older writers also see this reaching ahead to Jerusalem's later fall to the Romans. Greater privileges, when misused, bring greater punishment.

The siege would bring such terrible hunger that parents would eat their children, and children their parents. Moses had warned of this long before (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53). Lamentations 4:10 shows it really happened. Those who survived would be scattered in every direction.

"As surely as I live" is God's most solemn oath. His own life is the guarantee. The worst of their sins was filling His temple, His holy house, with idols. So God would turn His kind eye away and show no pity. Some see in these strong words a warning of the final judgment on all who never turn from their sin.

God now says without any picture what the three parts of hair meant. A third would die of plague and hunger inside the city. A third would fall by the sword outside the walls. A third would be scattered, with a sword still chasing them. No group would escape.

God speaks in human terms so we can understand. His long-held anger would be fully spent, and His justice satisfied. This is not a promise that the punishment would ease. It is a firm warning. When it happened, the people would know, too late, that God Himself had spoken through His prophet in His jealous love for His own glory. One source sees here a pointer to the cross, where God's wrath was poured out on Christ.
Jerusalem, once famous and honored, would become a ruin and a disgrace. Every traveler passing by would see it. The higher she had been raised, the deeper her shame would be when she fell.

Jerusalem would become something the nations mocked, and also a warning to them. Israel should have taught the nations to fear God by living well. Now they would learn it from her ruin. Other sinners would see what they too could expect from God. "I, the LORD, have spoken" seals the message as God's own word.

God pictures famine as deadly, poisoned arrows that kill wherever they hit. These arrows could be locusts, mildew, or anything else that ruins crops. God has more arrows in reserve than people expect. Cutting off their food means taking away the bread that life leans on, like a walking stick. Some say God can even make food fail to satisfy.

God piles up the dangers: famine, wild beasts, plague, bloodshed, and the sword. Wild animals multiply in an emptied land, and they would take away children. Some also see the beasts as a picture of the Babylonian armies. The warning is repeated in many forms to wake up careless hearts. The closing "I, the LORD, have spoken" reminds hearers that these were God's words, not the prophet's own.
